newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Afghan official says government may cede Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan official says government may cede Kabul.

text.p: An Afghan official said late on Thursday that his government was expected to arrange a formal handover of the capital of Kabul shortly in order to prevent a bloodbath.

Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai, Afghanistan's deputy foreign minister, said that in the face of attacks from the radical Islamic Taleban militia, the government had planned a "strategic retreat" to prevent civilian casualities.

The minister, who is attending the U.N. General Assembly session, spoke to Reuters Television shortly before witnesses in Kabul said Taleban forces had captured the city, meeting little resistance from government soldiers.

Ghafoorzai said government forces earlier had removed aircraft, including MiG fighters and helicopter gunships, tanks and armoured personnel to positions north of the capital as Taleban militia had captured strategic positions.
"The forces of Talebans managed to get themselves close to the centre of the city and the chief of the armed forces of the government Commander (Ahmad Shah) Masood decided to retreat," he said.
"There was a great possibiliity that (had) the government decided to resist and defend Kabul, there would definitely have been a bloodbath," he added.
"I think it was a very wise decision not to continue to resist because otherwise Kabul would have certainly turned into a disastrous situation," he said.
He said that President Burhanuddin Rabbani and his top advisers also were probably somewhere to the north of the city.
"I think by tomorrow (Friday) President Rabbani will announce a decision that there would be a transfer of power. To whom, we do not know."

Asked how power could be handed over to anyone but the Taleban, Ghafoorzai said King Zahir Shah, ousted in 1973 and now in Rome, had earlier this year expressed willingness to return. He added that the king had the respect of many parties, including the Taleban.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), in a statement released in New York, said there had been hundreds of casualties on both sides during the last two days.

It said the city's hospitals were inundated and that some of the wounded from Kabul being taken to Jalalabad. The ICRC organised a convoy on Wednesday to bringing in medical supplies from Pakistan to Jalalabad.

The Taleban controls more than half the central Asian country, which has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.
Emerging from the obscurity of religious schools in Pakistan two years ago, the group has been fighting to oust Rabbani's coalition government and impose a stricter Islamic order across Afghanistan.
